## Why this document exists

Before extracting data from sources (GBIF, NCBI, TRES bulletins), the literature
you read needs a **consistent, controlled set of tags** in Obsidian/Zotero. Without
this, you will end up with synonyms scattered across notes (e.g. `#formosensis`,
`#C.formosensis`, `#taiwan-wild-tea` all meaning the same thing), and you will have
to redo the tagging later — which costs more time than doing it right now.

This document is a **literal, step-by-step walkthrough**, using 5 real published
papers as worked examples. No botany or evolutionary biology background is assumed.
You only need to be able to read a title and abstract.

::: {.callout-note}
## What a "tag dimension" means
A *dimension* is a category you'll always want to filter by — like a column in a
spreadsheet. A *tag* is one specific value inside that column. "Organism" is a
dimension; `formosensis` is a tag inside it. You will derive both directly from
real papers in Action 2 below — you do not need to invent them from scratch.
:::

---

## The 5 worked-example papers

These are real, verifiable papers relevant to your project. You can substitute your
own papers later, but use these now so you have concrete material instead of a blank
page.

| # | Paper | Source |
|---|-------|--------|
| 1 | Su, Hsieh & Tsou (2009). "The confirmation of *Camellia formosensis* (Theaceae) as an independent species based on DNA sequence analyses." *Botanical Studies* 50(4):477–485. | [PDF](https://ejournal.sinica.edu.tw/bbas/content/2009/4/Bot504-11.pdf) |
| 2 | Wu et al. "The Plastome of *Camellia formosensis* (Theaceae) Reconfirms the Endemism of Taiwanese Wild Tea." | [TFRI](https://www.tfri.gov.tw/en/News_Content2.aspx?n=7589&s=32788) |
| 3 | "Development of STS and CAPS markers for variety identification and genetic diversity analysis of tea germplasm in Taiwan." *Botanical Studies* 55:12. | [Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1999-3110-55-12) |
| 4 | Study on "Influence of natural light intensities on growth and content of catechins and caffeine in *Camellia formosensis* leaves and tea infusion." | (ResearchGate listing) |
| 5 | International Camellia Register species entry for *Camellia formosensis*, including TTES cultivar lineage notes (TTES #18 "Ruby," TTES #24). | [Register](https://camellia.iflora.cn/Species/Detail?latin=Camellia+formosensis) |

::: {.callout-important}
## Evidence check before you proceed
Paper 1 is the taxonomic foundation of your whole project: it's the study that
established *C. formosensis* as its own species using nuclear DNA sequence
analysis (the RPB2 gene), separate from *C. sinensis* var. *sinensis* and var.
*assamica*. Everything downstream (TRES breeding, TTES cultivars) assumes this
species boundary. If you only read one paper before building your taxonomy, read
this one's abstract.
:::

---

## Action 1 — Gather the 5 papers (or your own equivalents)

**What to do:** Open each link above (or search Google Scholar / NCBI / GBIF for
your own 5–10 papers if you prefer). You only need the **title + abstract** for
each — do not read the full paper yet.

### Search keywords by topic direction

If you're sourcing your own papers instead of using the 5 above, here are concrete
search strings to use per topic area — these map directly to the dimensions
you'll build in Action 3, so searching across all four directions now gives you
a more balanced starting table.

**Taxonomy / species identity:**
- `"Camellia formosensis" taxonomy`
- `"Camellia formosensis" DNA sequence species`
- `Camellia sinensis var. assamica vs sinensis Taiwan`

**Genomics / molecular:**
- `"Camellia formosensis" plastome OR chloroplast genome`
- `Camellia formosensis genome sequencing`
- `tea plant Camellia genome NCBI`

**Lineage / breeding / cultivars:**
- `TTES cultivar Taiwan tea breeding`
- `"Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station" cultivar`
- `Qingxin Oolong cultivar lineage`
- `STS CAPS markers tea germplasm Taiwan`

**Chemistry / phytochemistry:**
- `Camellia formosensis catechin caffeine content`
- `Taiwan wild tea phytochemical composition`

**Cultivation / agronomy / geography:**
- `Camellia formosensis distribution Taiwan elevation`
- `Taiwan tea growing region GBIF occurrence`

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why search across all four directions, not just one
If you only search "Camellia formosensis genome," you'll end up with 8 genomics
papers and nothing on lineage or chemistry — your Action 2 table will look
lopsided, and you won't get a representative tag list. Pull 1–2 results from each
direction above instead of maximizing results from one search.
:::

**Time:** 10–15 minutes.

**Watch out for:** The temptation to start deeply reading paper 1 because it's
interesting. Resist — this stage is inventory, not comprehension. You're scanning,
not studying.

---

## Action 2 — Fill in a 4-column table, one row per paper

For each paper, answer four questions **in your own plain words** — no jargon
required, and nothing here requires you to evaluate the science:

1. **Organism** — which species or cultivar is this paper about?
2. **Method** — what kind of evidence did they generate (DNA sequencing, plant
   measurements, chemical analysis, historical records)?
3. **Pathway/topic** — what relationship does this paper inform (is it about
   ancestry/lineage, where it grows, its chemistry, or its species classification)?
4. **Notes** — anything that doesn't fit cleanly (flag it, don't force it)

### Worked example, filled in from the 5 papers above

| Paper | Organism | Method | Pathway/topic | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Su et al. 2009 | *C. formosensis* vs. *C. sinensis* var. *sinensis*/*assamica* | DNA sequencing (RPB2 nuclear gene) | Taxonomy (species classification) | Foundational species-naming paper |
| 2. Plastome paper | *C. formosensis* | DNA sequencing (chloroplast genome / plastome) | Taxonomy + lineage (molecular markers for future studies) | Confirms paper 1's conclusion independently |
| 3. STS/CAPS markers | Tea germplasm in Taiwan (multiple cultivars) | Genetic marker development (STS, CAPS — types of DNA-based ID tests) | Lineage (variety identification, genetic diversity) | Useful for your `HAS_GENOTYPE` relationship later |
| 4. Light intensity study | *C. formosensis* | Field/lab measurement (catechin & caffeine content under light conditions) | Chemistry (phytochemical content) | Not about lineage at all — pure chemistry |
| 5. Camellia Register entry | *C. formosensis* + TTES #18, TTES #24 (named cultivars) | Historical/registry record (not a primary research study) | Lineage (breeding history: wild species crossed into named cultivars) | This is the clearest real-world example of a `DERIVED_FROM` relationship in your schema — TTES #24 derived from wild *formosensis* populations |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why this table is the actual taxonomy-building step
You didn't invent "Taxonomy," "Lineage," and "Chemistry" as abstract categories —
you read them directly off 5 real papers. This is the core trick: **the categories
already exist in your sources; your job is to notice and name them, not invent
them.**
:::

**Time:** 20–25 minutes for 5 papers (less once you're warmed up).

---

## Action 3 — Turn each column into a tag list

Look down each column. Write the **distinct, deduplicated** values as a list.
This is mechanical — you're just removing repeats.

**From the Organism column:**

```
formosensis
sinensis-assamica
ttes-cultivar       (generic — use only when the specific cultivar/TTES number isn't named)
ttes-18             (specific cultivar, when named — "Ruby")
ttes-24             (specific cultivar, when named)
multi               (paper compares more than one organism, e.g. paper 1)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out for: synonym collision
Paper 5 names cultivars as "TTES #18" and "Ruby." These are the **same plant**.
Decide now: tags use the TTES number, not the common name, because TTES numbers
are the canonical registry identifiers TRES itself uses — common names like "Ruby"
or "Hong Yu" can vary by source. Keep a separate note (e.g. `_synonyms.md`) mapping
common names to TTES numbers; don't let the tag system absorb every synonym
directly.
:::

**From the Method column:**

```
genomics            (DNA/plastome sequencing — papers 1, 2)
genetic-markers      (STS/CAPS marker development — paper 3)
phytochemistry       (catechin/caffeine content — paper 4)
historical-record    (registry/bulletin entries, not primary research — paper 5)
```

**From the Pathway/topic column:**

```
taxonomy     (species classification — papers 1, 2)
lineage      (breeding/ancestry — papers 3, 5)
chemistry    (phytochemical profile — paper 4)
cultivation  (growing region/agronomy — not yet seen in these 5, but reserve it; you will hit it in TRES agronomy bulletins)
```

**Time:** 10 minutes. This step is just deduplication — no new judgment calls.

---

## Action 4 — Write the taxonomy into one Obsidian note

Create a note called `_taxonomy.md` and pin/star it. Use Obsidian's nested tag
syntax (`#dimension/value`) — this renders hierarchically in the tag pane and lets
you query either the parent (`#organism`) or a specific child (`#organism/ttes-24`)
with Dataview.

```markdown
# Tagging Taxonomy
*Last reviewed: <date>*

## #organism
- formosensis — wild Taiwanese tea species (Su et al. 2009)
- sinensis-assamica — introduced Assamica lineage
- ttes-18 — named cultivar "Ruby" (TRES registry)
- ttes-24 — named cultivar bred from wild formosensis populations
- ttes-cultivar — generic, use only if specific TTES number is unknown
- multi — paper covers more than one organism

## #method
- genomics — DNA/plastome sequencing
- genetic-markers — STS/CAPS or similar marker development
- phytochemistry — chemical composition analysis
- historical-record — registry entries, TRES bulletins, non-primary-research sources

## #pathway
- taxonomy — species classification questions
- lineage — breeding/ancestry relationships
- chemistry — phytochemical profile
- cultivation — growing region, agronomic practice

## Open/uncertain
- (papers that don't fit — review monthly, see Action 5 rule)
```

**Time:** 10 minutes to write this up cleanly from Action 3's lists.

---

## Action 5 — Set your rule for new/uncertain values *now*

You will hit a 6th paper that doesn't fit any value above. Decide the rule before
it happens, so you don't have to think mid-reading-session:

- **Rule:** Tag it `#organism/unclear` (or the equivalent for whichever dimension
  doesn't fit) and move on immediately.
- **Batch review:** Once a month, look at everything tagged `unclear` and decide
  then whether it needs a new permanent tag value or was a one-off.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why batching beats real-time decisions
If you stop to deliberate "is this a new tag or not?" every time you hit an edge
case, tagging stops being a 2-minute task per paper and becomes a research project
in itself. Given your ~3 hr/week budget, protect your reading time — defer the
taxonomy edits.
:::

---

## Action 6 — Tag the 5 papers, and only the 5 papers, right now

Go into Zotero/Obsidian and apply tags to these 5 papers using **only** the values
written in `_taxonomy.md`. Example for paper 5 (Camellia Register entry):

```
#organism/ttes-24 #organism/formosensis #method/historical-record #pathway/lineage
```

This is also your taxonomy's first real test. If, by paper 5, you already want to
add a tag that's not on the list, that's useful signal — but don't add it live;
note it and move to Action 5's batch-review rule.

**Time:** 5 minutes for 5 papers.

---

## What you should have at the end (checklist)

- [ ] `_taxonomy.md` exists with 3 dimensions and a controlled list of values for each
- [ ] 5 papers tagged using only those values
- [ ] A decision recorded on cultivar tagging (TTES number vs. common name) — and a
      stub `_synonyms.md` note started, even if empty
- [ ] A rule written down for handling new/unclear values (batch monthly)

**Total time for this whole document, start to finish: ~60–75 minutes**, in one
sitting or split across two sessions.

---

## The end-to-end workflow: Zotero → Obsidian → Claude assist → tags

Once the taxonomy exists, here is the repeatable loop you'll run for every new
paper. This assumes your existing setup: Zotero (Better BibTeX + Zotero Integration
plugin) and Obsidian (Dataview, Templater).

```
1. Zotero        →  2. Obsidian literature note  →  3. Claude assist  →  4. Tag + file
   (capture)          (auto-generated via plugin)      (summarize/extract)   (apply taxonomy)
```

### Step 1 — Capture the paper in Zotero

Add the PDF/citation to Zotero as you normally would (browser connector, manual
entry, or DOI lookup). This is your system of record for the citation itself —
Obsidian should never hold the canonical bibliographic data, only notes *about*
the paper.

### Step 2 — Generate the literature note in Obsidian

Use the Zotero Integration plugin to pull the paper into Obsidian as a new note,
using your Templater template (the one with fields for organism, gene IDs, dataset
accession numbers — the bioinformatics-tuned template you're building). This gives
you a note with the citation metadata already filled in, and empty fields waiting
for content.

### Step 3 — Claude assist, inside that same note

This is where Claude does extraction/summarization work — but with two hard rules,
given your principle that AI output must stay clearly distinct from your own
analysis:

- **Label everything Claude produces.** Use a literal heading like `## AI-Assisted
  Summary` or an inline tag like `#ai-generated`, so six months from now you can
  tell at a glance what's Claude's extraction versus your own reading notes.
- **Claude extracts facts, you make judgments.** Ask Claude to pull out things that
  are explicitly stated in the abstract/methods — organism, method type, gene IDs,
  accession numbers, sample size — not to infer significance or relevance. That
  interpretive layer is yours.

**Concrete prompt pattern to use inside the Obsidian note** (paste the abstract,
then ask):

> "From this abstract only, extract: (1) organism studied, (2) method type
> (genomics/morphology/field-survey/historical-record/etc.), (3) any gene IDs or
> accession numbers mentioned, (4) one sentence stating the main finding. Do not
> infer anything not explicitly stated."

This keeps Claude's output narrow, factual, and auditable — which matters if this
note ever ends up referenced in a BISS manuscript.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out for: letting Claude pick the tags
Don't ask Claude to "tag this paper" freely — it doesn't know your controlled
vocabulary and will invent plausible-sounding tags that don't match
`_taxonomy.md`. Instead, ask Claude to extract the four facts above, and **you**
map them to tag values yourself (or ask Claude to pick *only* from a pasted list
of your existing tag values — never an open-ended ask).
:::

### Step 4 — Apply tags from `_taxonomy.md` and file the note

Using the facts Claude extracted in Step 3, apply tags manually:

```
#organism/formosensis #method/genomics #pathway/taxonomy #ai-generated
```

If a value doesn't exist yet in your taxonomy, follow the Action 5 rule from
earlier in this document — tag `unclear` and batch-review monthly, rather than
deciding live.

### Why this division of labor works

- **Zotero** owns citations (stable, structured, never touched by AI)
- **Obsidian** owns your synthesis and the taxonomy (your judgment, your tags)
- **Claude** owns narrow, auditable extraction (clearly labeled, never freely
  tagging or interpreting)

This mirrors the same separation you're already building into the data
pipeline — extraction/normalization is mechanical and reviewable, interpretation
is a separate, deliberate step. The literature workflow is a smaller-scale dry run
of the same discipline.

---

## Objective of this phase, stated plainly

This entire document covers **one phase** of the tea heritage knowledge graph
project: building the **knowledge management layer** — the taxonomy, synonym
mapping, and literature workflow that everything downstream depends on.

**What this phase is for:** giving every paper you read a consistent, retrievable
identity (which organism, what evidence type, what relationship) *before* any
data gets extracted into DuckDB/Neo4j. The categories you define here
(`#organism`, `#method`, `#pathway`) are not busywork — they are a dry run of the
same boundaries your normalization layer will need (cultivar synonym resolution,
entity types for nodes). Get them stable now, cheaply, in Obsidian; avoid
re-deriving them under pressure later while also debugging a Cypher load script.

**What this phase is explicitly NOT:** data extraction, OCR pipeline work, schema
design for Neo4j nodes/edges, or anything touching DuckDB. Those are the *next*
phase. If you find yourself wanting to start the OCR pipeline or design `Cultivar`
node properties while still tagging papers — that's scope creep across phases.
Finish this one first; the milestone below tells you when.

---

## Milestone: Knowledge Management Layer Complete

You're done with this phase — and clear to move to ETL/data extraction — when
**all** of these are true:

- [ ] `_taxonomy.md` exists with all dimensions (organism, method, pathway, +
      cultivation if it's shown up) and each has a stable, named list of values
- [ ] `_synonyms.md` exists with at least the cultivar name ↔ TTES-code mappings
      you've hit so far (doesn't need to be exhaustive — just started and real)
- [ ] **10–15 papers tagged** (not just the 5 worked examples in this document) —
      this is the real test, because it's enough volume to surface whether your
      taxonomy holds up or needs revision
- [ ] You've hit at least **one genuine "doesn't fit" case** and handled it with
      the `unclear` + batch-review rule rather than improvising a new category on
      the spot — proves the rule works under real conditions, not just in theory
- [ ] The Zotero → Obsidian → Claude → tag workflow has been run **end-to-end at
      least 3 times** by you personally — Claude assists, you label, you tag
- [ ] The Templater literature note template (organism, gene IDs, accession
      numbers) is finalized and is what new notes are created from — not still
      being redesigned per-paper

### What "complete" does NOT require

- A perfect taxonomy. It will evolve — that's what the monthly `unclear` review
  is for.
- Every paper you'll ever read tagged. 10–15 is enough signal; the rest gets
  tagged as you go, using the now-stable system.
- Zero ambiguity. One or two `unclear` tags sitting in the batch-review queue is
  healthy, not a blocker.

### Signal you're NOT done yet

If you're still **renaming or restructuring dimensions** (e.g., realizing
"method" should actually split into two axes) past paper #10, the taxonomy
hasn't stabilized — finish that churn before starting ETL. Your DuckDB staging
schema and normalization layer will lean on these same category boundaries;
cultivar synonym resolution is literally the same problem as `_synonyms.md`,
just at production scale.

### Realistic timeline

Given a ~3 hr/week budget, this checklist is **roughly 2–3 weeks** of light,
steady work — most of it is reading + tagging volume, not new decisions.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tracking progress without manual checking
Add a Dataview query to `_taxonomy.md` that counts tagged papers per dimension
and surfaces anything still tagged `unclear`:

```dataview
TABLE length(rows) as "Count"
FROM #organism OR #method OR #pathway
GROUP BY file.tags
```

And a dedicated query to flag your review queue:

```dataview
LIST
FROM #organism/unclear OR #method/unclear OR #pathway/unclear
```

Check this monthly as part of the batch-review rule from Action 5 — it turns the
milestone checklist above from something you track in your head into something
Obsidian tracks for you.
:::

---

## What comes next

Once this taxonomy exists, the next step is the **entity/relation schema** for
Neo4j — i.e., deciding exactly what properties a `Cultivar` node or `Region` node
has. Notice that Action 3 above (organism tag list) and Action 4 (cultivar IDs vs.
common names) are *previews* of that schema work — you are not duplicating effort,
you're front-loading decisions you need anyway.
